question: Explain the difference between transverse and longitudinal waves.
mark_scheme: Transverse: oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer (1); longitudinal: oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer (1).

question: A sound wave has a frequency of 340 Hz and a wavelength of 1 m. Calculate the wave speed.
mark_scheme: Wave speed = frequency × wavelength (1); v = 340 × 1 = 340 m/s (1).

question: State two properties that all electromagnetic waves share.
mark_scheme: Any two from: all travel at the same speed in a vacuum (3 × 10⁸ m/s) (1); all are transverse waves (1); all can travel through a vacuum (1); all transfer energy (1).

question: Explain why refraction occurs when light passes from air into glass.
mark_scheme: Light slows down when it enters glass (1); because glass is denser than air (1); the change in speed causes the light to change direction / bend towards the normal (1).

question: Describe how an echo is produced and state one use of echoes.
mark_scheme: Sound reflects off a surface and returns to the listener (1); use: sonar / ultrasound imaging / measuring distances (1).

question: Explain why sound cannot travel through space.
mark_scheme: Sound is a longitudinal/mechanical wave (1); it requires particles/a medium to travel through, and space is a vacuum with no particles (1).

question: Explain the conditions needed for total internal reflection to occur.
mark_scheme: Light must be travelling from a denser medium to a less dense medium (1); the angle of incidence must be greater than the critical angle (1); all the light is then reflected back into the denser medium rather than refracting out (1).

question: Describe the properties of a perfect black body.
mark_scheme: Absorbs all electromagnetic radiation that falls on it — reflects none (1); is also the best possible emitter of radiation (1).

question: Explain how the temperature of an object affects the radiation it emits.
mark_scheme: All objects emit electromagnetic radiation (1); as temperature increases, more radiation is emitted (1); higher temperature objects emit radiation at shorter wavelengths / higher frequencies (1).

question: State one use and one harmful effect of ultraviolet radiation.
mark_scheme: Use: sterilisation / fluorescent lamps / detecting forged banknotes (1); harmful effect: skin cancer / eye damage / sunburn (1).

question: A water wave has a wave speed of 6 m/s and a wavelength of 0.03 m. Calculate its frequency.
Describe how X-rays are used in medical imaging and why they are suitable for this purpose.
mark_scheme: X-rays pass through soft tissue but are absorbed by denser materials like bone (1); this creates an image showing the skeleton / dense structures inside the body (1).

question: Explain the difference between transverse and longitudinal waves, using sound and light as examples. Include a description of compressions and rarefactions in your answer.
mark_scheme: Transverse: oscillations perpendicular to direction of energy transfer — light is an example (1); longitudinal: oscillations parallel to direction of energy transfer — sound is an example (1); compressions: regions where particles are pushed closer together (1); rarefactions: regions where particles are spread further apart (1).

question: Describe the electromagnetic spectrum. Include the order of waves, their relative wavelengths and frequencies, and give one use for each of three different wave types.
mark_scheme: Correct order: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma (1); frequency increases / wavelength decreases from radio to gamma (1); any three waves with correct uses, e.g. radio — broadcasting, microwaves — cooking/communication, infrared — remote controls, UV — sterilisation, X-rays — medical imaging, gamma — cancer treatment (1 mark per correct use, up to 2 marks).

question: Explain what happens to light when it travels from air into a glass block and back out again. Include refraction and the conditions for total internal reflection in your answer.
mark_scheme: Light slows down entering glass and bends towards the normal (refraction) (1); light speeds up leaving glass and bends away from the normal (1); if the angle of incidence inside the glass exceeds the critical angle (1); total internal reflection occurs — all light reflects back inside the glass (1); application e.g. optical fibres use total internal reflection to carry light signals (1).

question: Evaluate the risks and benefits of using electromagnetic radiation in medicine. Refer to at least two different types of EM radiation in your answer.
mark_scheme: X-rays: benefit — image bones and dense tissue for diagnosis (1); risk — ionising radiation can damage cells/cause cancer (1); gamma rays: benefit — used in radiotherapy to kill cancer cells / sterilise medical equipment (1); risk — can damage healthy tissue / cause mutations (1); infrared/UV may also be credited with appropriate use and risk; well-reasoned conclusion weighing benefits against risks (1).

question: Explain what is meant by a perfect black body and how black body radiation relates to the temperature of stars. Include how scientists can use this information.
mark_scheme: Perfect black body absorbs all radiation — reflects none — and is the best possible emitter (1); all objects emit radiation; hotter objects emit more radiation and at shorter wavelengths (1); stars behave approximately as black bodies (1); hotter stars emit peak radiation at shorter wavelengths — appear blue/white; cooler stars appear red/orange (1); scientists can determine the temperature of a star from the peak wavelength of its emitted radiation (1).

question: Evaluate the use of ultrasound in medicine compared to X-rays. In your answer, explain how ultrasound works, the advantages and disadvantages of each method, and suggest when each would be most appropriate.
mark_scheme: Ultrasound: high frequency sound waves (above 20,000 Hz) sent into the body (1); reflected at boundaries between tissues; time taken to return used to build an image (1); advantage of ultrasound: non-ionising — no risk of cell damage / safe for use in pregnancy (1); disadvantage: less clear images of bone/dense structures than X-rays (1); X-rays: better for imaging bones and dense tissue / faster to use (1); disadvantage: ionising radiation — repeated exposure increases cancer risk (1). Award mark for well-reasoned conclusion about appropriate use of each.

question: A communications engineer is designing a system to transmit data over long distances. Evaluate the suitability of using radio waves, microwaves, and optical fibres (using visible light or infrared) for this purpose.
mark_scheme: Radio waves: long wavelength, can diffract around obstacles and follow curvature of Earth — good for broadcasting over large areas (1); can be affected by interference / lower data capacity (1); microwaves: used for satellite communication — pass through atmosphere (1); require line of sight / can be absorbed by water/rain (1); optical fibres: use total internal reflection to carry light/infrared signals (1); very high data capacity / fast / not affected by electromagnetic interference — suitable for internet/phone cables (1). Award mark for justified conclusion recommending a method for a specific context.
